title: Andal's dawn vow
hookLine: a list of things a group of girls won't do for a month, and what they lean on when they finally reach Krishna's door
carry: keep the vow, but lean on grace, not merit
tomorrow: three strangers, one tiny shelter, rain. who's the fourth?

cards: No ghee. No milk. A bath before dawn.
No kohl on the eyes, no flowers in the hair. That's part of a list, kept by the girls of Krishna's cowherd village as they set out on a vow for the month of Margazhi. The list is a hymn.
Andal, one of the Alvars, sang it in her Tiruppavai, the song of the dawn vow. Year three walked with those girls as they woke each other in the dark and went knocking at Krishna's door.
Today, two other pages of the same song: the rules they keep on the way, and what they say about themselves when they arrive.

teach.h: BATHE BEFORE DAWN. NO GHEE, NO MILK.
teach.b: Early in the hymn, the girls set out the vow. They'll bathe before dawn. They'll go without ghee and milk.
They won't line their eyes or put flowers in their hair.

teach.h: NO HARMFUL WORDS. GIVE WHAT YOU CAN.
teach.b: They won't do what shouldn't be done, and they won't go carrying harmful words about anyone. Then the list turns from giving up to giving: alms and gifts, as much as they're able.
So the vow trims the comforts, guards the tongue, and opens the hand. At the end of the hymn, they finally stand before Krishna. They don't mention the cold baths or the missed ghee.
We follow the cows into the woods and eat there, they say. We're a cowherd clan with no learning at all. Our one good fortune is that you were born among us.
Then the line Sri Vaishnava teachers keep coming back to: the bond between you and us can't be undone here, even if someone tried.
We're children who don't know any better, they add; if, out of love, we called you by small names, don't be angry. A month of discipline, and at the door they don't hold it up.

Sri Vaishnava teachers read a big teaching here: you don't reach God by stacking up merit. You're held by the relationship, and by grace. Keep the vow; it gets you out of bed in the dark and shapes you.
Just don't bring it to the door as a bill.

how: In the month of Margazhi, Sri Vaishnava temples and households recite Andal's Tiruppavai before dawn, and teachers explain its verses on the rules of the vow and on the bond with the Lord that can't be undone.

games.q: you're one of the girls. a month of cold baths and missed ghee, and now you stand at Krishna's door. what do you lean on?
o: everything we gave up this month.
our learning and our good deeds.
the bond between us, which can't be undone.
games.why: at the end of the hymn the girls call themselves cowherds with no learning, and say the bond between them and Krishna can't be undone.

practice: Bring to mind someone you're close to, or God if you pray, and notice any urge to arrive with a list: what you've done for them, how hard you've tried, what you've given up.
Let the list go quiet, one item at a time, and rest in the plain fact of the bond, with nothing to show. If a small, fond name for them comes to mind, let it come.

wordCard.voice: The Alvar hymns. Today, Andal's dawn vow: comforts trimmed, the tongue guarded, the hand open, and at the door, only the bond.

orig.note: Tamil: the name of Andal's hymn of the dawn vow. Tamil, not Sanskrit, is the language of the Alvar hymns.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the vow, but lean on grace, not merit. A month of cold baths, and at the door, only the bond. Until tomorrow.
